title: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)
summary: A securities-fraud complaint must support a cogent inference of scienter at least as compelling as plausible opposing inferences.
notes: This is the special statutory securities test. It should not be imported as an automatic requirement that every ordinary Rule 8 complaint establish an equally strong comparative inference.

sections.Parties: Investors sued Tellabs and its chief executive concerning statements about products and the company’s financial performance.
sections.Material Facts: The complaint alleged that public statements about demand, products, and revenues misrepresented the company’s actual position. It drew on statements attributed to confidential sources and other circumstances to support the contention that defendants acted with the required state of mind. The dispute on review concerned how strongly the facts had to support that inference at the pleading stage.
sections.Procedural History: The lower courts applied differing descriptions of the required inference. The Supreme Court vacated the court of appeals’ judgment and remanded for application of its stated standard.
sections.Issue: How should a court decide whether the pleaded facts create the strong inference of scienter required by the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act?
sections.Holding: The inference must be cogent and at least as compelling as any plausible nonculpable explanation, assessed from the allegations as a whole.
sections.Reasoning: The statute added a requirement beyond ordinary pleading. The Court required a holistic evaluation rather than judging each allegation in isolation. It also required comparison: an inference can seem persuasive alone yet be weak when a convincing innocent explanation accounts for the same facts. Conversely, the plaintiff need not show an irrefutable inference. This comparative approach implements the statutory requirement while leaving factual adjudication for later proceedings if the complaint survives.

learning.why: A securities-fraud complaint must support a cogent inference of scienter at least as compelling as plausible opposing inferences.

topics.cp-securities-pleading: The PSLRA required a strong inference of the relevant state of mind.
topics.cp-inferences: The court had to compare the inference of scienter with plausible nonfraudulent explanations.
topics.cp-pleading-proof: The heightened statutory pleading test did not decide which account was true.

learning.separateOpinions: Justices Scalia and Alito wrote separately concerning the strength and formulation of the required inference. Their positions should not replace the Court’s at-least-as-compelling formulation.

mnemonic.rationale: A securities fraud pleaded with particularity
